title: Looking back: the ragas

lines: A LULLABY AT NOON SOUNDS WRONG.
HOW IT WAS MEANT TO BE HEARD.
cards: Some songs belong to a time of day. A lullaby at noon sounds wrong. A wedding song at a funeral would be unbearable.
The Sikh tradition built that into the scripture itself. Over the year you've met hymns of praise, of longing, of warning, of joy, each under a heading that named its raga before anything else.
So as this year of the ways of the Guru begins to close, the looking back starts with the sound under the words: how it was meant to be heard.

teach.b: First, the headings. You met this a week ago: after the opening prayers, the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raga. The hymns sat under raga names, like a door you walk through before you hear a word.

teach.h: A RAGA IS A MOOD AND AN HOUR.
teach.b: Second, a raga is a mood. Musicians in the tradition speak of each one having its own color and its own hour. In Sikh practice, Asa di Var is sung in the early morning.
Tradition links Basant with spring and Malar with the rains. The Word doesn't change, but it arrives dressed for the moment. Third, the moods are honest.

teach.h: TUKHARI: THE SONG OF THE MONTHS.
teach.b: In Raag Tukhari, Guru Nanak's song of the months walks through the year as a bride longing for her beloved: the heat, the rain, the cold, each month its own ache, until union comes. Longing gets its own music.
So does warning, so does celebration. Nobody is asked to fake a mood they're not in.

The same Name is sung in grief and in joy, at dawn and at night, in spring and in the rains. There's a raga for whatever state you walk in with, which means no mood has to be fixed before coming near the Word.
You bring the mood. The music meets it.

how: In gurdwaras, ragis (kirtan musicians) sing hymns in the raga named at their head, and Sikh practice sets particular hymns, such as Asa di Var in the morning, for particular times.

o: regretting the year's missed days and mistakes
a rule against moving on until all is learned
pausing to see the year whole, starting with its music

games.q: looking back, the ragas: tap the pairs.
p: Guru Nanak's song of the months

s: every raga in the Granth carries the same mood
each has its own color and hour: morning, spring, rain, longing.
Guru Nanak's song of the months is full of longing
in Tukhari, a bride aches through the months until union comes.
you have to be in a calm mood before you come near the Word
one Word, many moods: there's music for whatever state you bring.

games.q: you're grieving, and a friend asks which hymn the musicians should sing. what does the idea of the ragas suggest?
o: any hymn; the tune doesn't matter.
a hymn in a mood that meets grief where it is.
only cheerful hymns, to force the mood up.
games.why: the Granth gives longing and sorrow their own music; nobody is asked to fake a mood they're not in.

practice: Name your mood right now, honestly, in one word, tired, hopeful, restless, sad, light, without correcting it.
Then ask which hour and season it belongs to, dawn or deep night, spring or the cold, and let them settle around you, the way a raga heading sits over a hymn.
Breathe inside it, and notice whether the mood shifts or just feels accompanied.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. At the year's close, the ragas: hymns under a mood's name, one Word sung for every state you're in. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: raag, a musical mode with its own mood, under which the Granth's hymns are set.

carryVoice: Your line: many moods. Dawn or deep night, there's music for it. Go gently.
